text:
Embedding indexes map each passage into a vector representation. After source documents change, stale vectors can continue to return obsolete evidence. Re-encoding changed passages and atomically swapping the refreshed index prevents stale retrieval.

A separate cache may still hold old answers. Cache invalidation should therefore follow the index refresh so that retrieval and generation observe the same content version.

First-stage retrieval should favor recall and can return dozens of candidates. A cross-encoder reranker spends more compute on those candidates to improve ordering. Teams often cap the candidate count because reranking latency grows with the number of passages scored.

When the latency budget is tight, batching and smaller candidate sets reduce cost. The quality trade-off should be measured at a fixed end-to-end budget.

Remote deployments require warming model weights before serving traffic. The startup checklist verifies local artifacts, opens the read-only index, and runs one retrieval health probe before accepting requests.

Power interruptions are common in isolated sites, so the service persists a checkpoint and can resume without rebuilding every artifact.

Remote deployments load model weights before serving traffic. The startup checklist verifies local artifacts, opens the read-only index, and checks network connectivity before accepting requests.

High humidity can damage edge hardware, so the service records sensor warnings and rotates to a spare node when required.

Overlapping chunks can preserve evidence that crosses a chunk boundary. The same overlap also repeats source tokens in the retrieved context. At a fixed context window, repeated tokens reduce the budget available for distinct evidence.

Sentence-aware chunks avoid cutting sentences in half. Paragraph-aware chunks preserve wider local structure but may be too coarse for focused retrieval.
